source_refs.note: Practice MCQs written from Chapter 5 (PDF 95-116, printed 95-116); not printed in the book. Based on the chapter's text, tables, boxes and worked examples (numericals with changed values); none repeats the chapter exercise. Drafts needing academic review.

blocks.text: Practice MCQs for the whole of Chapter 5 (States and Phases of Matter), arranged by the chapter's sections. Each question has one correct answer with a short explanation; numerical questions show the working.

blocks.prompt: 1 Matter exists in how many states?
blocks.explanation: Matter exists in four states: solid, liquid, gas and plasma (5.1).

book_ref.quote: Matter exists in four states i.e., solid, liquid, gas and plasma.

blocks.prompt: 2 The simplest form of matter is the:
blocks.explanation: The chapter states that the simplest form of matter is the gaseous state (5.1).

book_ref.quote: The simplest form of matter is the gaseous state

blocks.prompt: 3 Liquids are less common than the other states because the liquid state:

options.text: exists only at very high pressure
exists only within a narrow range of temperature and pressure

blocks.explanation: A liquid state can exist only within a relatively narrow range of temperature and pressure (5.1).

book_ref.quote: the liquid state of any substance can exist only within a relatively narrow range of temperature and pressure

blocks.prompt: 4 The volume of a gas sample is equal to:

options.text: the total volume of its molecules
half the volume of the container

blocks.explanation: Gases have no definite shape or volume; the volume of a gas is the volume of the container (5.1).

book_ref.quote: The volume of a gas is the volume of the container.

blocks.prompt: 5 Nearly what percentage of the volume of a gas is empty space?
blocks.explanation: Gas molecules are widely separated; nearly 99.9% of the volume is empty space, so gases are easily compressed (5.1).

book_ref.quote: most of the volume of the gas is empty space (nearly 99.9%)

blocks.prompt: 6 Cooling caused by the sudden expansion of a gas is called:
blocks.explanation: Cooling on sudden expansion of gases is called the Joule-Thomson effect (5.1).

book_ref.quote: When sudden expansion of gases occurs cooling takes place. It is called Joule-Thomson effect.

blocks.prompt: 7 The pressure of a gas is due to:

options.text: collisions of gas molecules with the walls of the container
vibration of molecules about mean positions

blocks.explanation: Gas pressure arises from collisions of its molecules with the container walls (5.1).

book_ref.quote: Pressure of a gas is due to the collisions of gas molecules with the walls of the container.

blocks.prompt: 8 According to the properties of gases, an ideal gas has:

options.text: large particle volume and strong forces
zero particle volume and negligible intermolecular forces

blocks.explanation: Ideal gases have zero particle volume and negligible intermolecular forces (5.1).

book_ref.quote: There are negligible intermolecular forces in ideal gases.

blocks.prompt: 9 Gas laws describe the relationship of the volume of a given amount of gas with:
blocks.explanation: Gas laws relate the volume of a given amount of gas to the prevailing temperature and pressure (5.2).

book_ref.quote: The gas laws describe the relationships between volume of a given amount of gas

blocks.prompt: 10 According to Boyle's law, V ∝ 1/P when:

options.text: n and P are held constant
n and T are held constant
P and T are held constant

blocks.explanation: Boyle's law: V ∝ 1/P when n and T are constant (equation 1, 5.2).

book_ref.quote: According to Boyle’s law.

blocks.prompt: 11 Which relation is Charles' law?

options.text: V ∝ T at constant n and P
V ∝ 1/P at constant n and T
V ∝ n at constant P and T

blocks.explanation: Charles' law: V ∝ T when n and P are held constant (equation 2, 5.2).

book_ref.quote: According to Charles’ law

blocks.prompt: 12 Avogadro's law states that at constant temperature and pressure the volume of a gas is directly proportional to its:
blocks.explanation: Avogadro's law: V ∝ n at constant P and T (5.2).

book_ref.quote: According to Avogadro’s law volume of the given gas at constant temperature and pressure

blocks.prompt: 13 The value of the ideal gas constant R given in the chapter is:
blocks.explanation: R, the ideal gas constant, is 0.0821 atm dm³ K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ (5.2).

book_ref.quote: Its value is 0.0821 atm dm³ K⁻¹ mol⁻¹.

blocks.prompt: 14 The ideal gas equation is:
blocks.explanation: Joining Boyle's, Charles' and Avogadro's laws gives V = R nT/P, i.e. PV = nRT, equation (4) (5.2).

book_ref.quote: The equation (4) is called the ideal gas equation.

blocks.prompt: 15 Combining the three gas laws when no variable is kept constant gives:
blocks.explanation: V ∝ 1/P, V ∝ T and V ∝ n combine to V ∝ nT/P (5.2).

book_ref.quote: If we think for a moment that none of the variables are to be kept constant

blocks.prompt: 16 How many moles of a gas occupy 8.21 dm³ at 2 atm and 400 K? (R = 0.0821 atm dm³ K⁻¹ mol⁻¹)

book_ref.quote: The constant suggested is ‘R’ which is called Ideal gas constant.

blocks.prompt: 17 What volume is occupied by 2 mol of an ideal gas at 27 °C and 3 atm? (R = 0.0821 atm dm³ K⁻¹ mol⁻¹)

book_ref.quote: It is a matter of common observation that when external conditions of temperature and pressure are changed

blocks.prompt: 18 0.25 mol of a gas is kept in a 5 dm³ vessel at 127 °C. Its pressure is: (R = 0.0821 atm dm³ K⁻¹ mol⁻¹)

book_ref.quote: all the above three relationships can be joined together as:

blocks.prompt: 19 Putting n = m/M in the ideal gas equation gives:
blocks.explanation: With n = m/M, equation (4) becomes PV = mRT/M, equation (5) (5.2).

book_ref.quote: Putting n = m/M in equation (4)

blocks.prompt: 20 The relative molecular mass of a gas is calculated from:
blocks.explanation: Rearranging PV = mRT/M gives M = mRT/PV; at the molecular level this is Mᵣ = mRT/PV, equation (7) (5.2).

book_ref.quote: Equation (4) can be employed to calculate the relative molecular mass of a gas

blocks.prompt: 21 3.2 g of a gas occupies 2.46 dm³ at 27 °C and 1 atm. Its relative molecular mass is: (R = 0.0821 atm dm³ K⁻¹ mol⁻¹)

book_ref.quote: At molecular level, the molar mass becomes relative molecular mass of a compound

blocks.prompt: 22 1.28 g of a gas occupies 0.448 dm³ at 0 °C and 1 atm. What is its molar mass? (R = 0.0821 atm dm³ K⁻¹ mol⁻¹)

book_ref.quote: This is achieved by rearranging equation (4)

blocks.prompt: 23 In the equation PV = mRT/M, the symbol m stands for:

options.text: mass of the gas in grams

blocks.explanation: m = mass in g and M = molar mass of the gas (5.2).

book_ref.quote: Where m = mass in g and M = molar mass of the gas

blocks.prompt: 24 0.88 g of a gas occupies 0.985 dm³ at 27 °C and 0.5 atm. Its relative molecular mass is closest to: (R = 0.0821 atm dm³ K⁻¹ mol⁻¹)

book_ref.quote: Determine the relative molecular mass of the gas.

blocks.prompt: 25 To use Mᵣ = mRT/PV with R = 0.0821 atm dm³ K⁻¹ mol⁻¹, a temperature of −23 °C must be written as:
blocks.explanation: Temperature must be in kelvin: −23 + 273 = 250 K (as −73 °C was written 200 K in Sample Problem 5.1) (5.2).

book_ref.quote: Solution: The molecular mass of the gas can be calculated by using the formula: M = mRT/PV

blocks.prompt: 26 Compared with gases, the rate of diffusion in liquids is:
blocks.explanation: Liquids diffuse like gases, but much more slowly (5.3).

book_ref.quote: the rate of diffusion in liquids is much lower than that in gases

blocks.prompt: 27 Liquids are about how many times less compressible than gases?
blocks.explanation: Liquids are 10⁵ times less compressible than gases but about 10 times more compressible than solids (5.3).

book_ref.quote: Liquids are 10⁵ times less compressible than gases

blocks.prompt: 28 Compared with solids, liquids are:
blocks.explanation: Liquids are about 10 times more compressible than solids (5.3).

book_ref.quote: but about 10 times more compressible than solids

blocks.prompt: 29 Evidence for the free motion of liquid molecules is:
blocks.explanation: Diffusion among miscible liquids shows that liquid molecules move freely; this also lets liquids flow (5.3).

book_ref.quote: Diffusion among the miscible liquids is an evidence for the free motion of liquid molecules.

blocks.prompt: 30 There are little spaces among liquid molecules because:

options.text: molecules do not move at all
molecules are arranged in a crystal lattice

blocks.explanation: Relatively stronger intermolecular forces keep liquid molecules close (5.3).

book_ref.quote: There are little spaces among liquid molecules because of relatively stronger intermolecular forces.

blocks.prompt: 31 On heating, the expansion of a liquid is:

options.text: negligible compared with that of gases

blocks.explanation: Liquids expand on heating, but negligibly compared with gases (5.3).

book_ref.quote: However, this expansion is negligible compare to that in gases.

blocks.prompt: 32 According to kinetic molecular theory, a liquid changes into a solid when:

options.text: the kinetic energy of its molecules is decreased by cooling
its kinetic energy is increased by heating

blocks.explanation: A liquid becomes a solid when its KE is decreased (cooling) and vapour when KE is increased (heating) (5.3).

book_ref.quote: a liquid is converted into a solid by decreasing its kinetic energy (on cooling)

blocks.prompt: 33 Which of the following is NOT one of the three intermolecular forces described for liquids?
blocks.explanation: The three forces named are id-id (London), permanent dipole-permanent dipole forces and hydrogen bonding (5.4).

book_ref.quote: Three types of such forces are mentioned here.

blocks.text: 5.4.1 Instantaneous dipole-induced dipole forces (London dispersion forces)

blocks.prompt: 34 The momentary force of attraction between an instantaneous dipole and an induced dipole is called:
blocks.explanation: This momentary attraction is the instantaneous dipole-induced dipole (London dispersion) force (5.4.1).

book_ref.quote: The momentary force of attraction between an instantaneous dipole and an induced dipole

blocks.prompt: 35 Among the molecules of a non-polar compound, the intermolecular forces present are:
blocks.explanation: Instantaneous dipole-induced dipole (London) forces are the only forces among molecules of non-polar compounds (5.4.1).

book_ref.quote: These are only forces that exist among the molecules of non-polar compounds.

blocks.prompt: 36 London dispersion forces are stronger in larger molecules because:

options.text: their electronic cloud is more easily dispersed and polarised

blocks.explanation: In a larger atom or molecule the electron cloud is more easily dispersed and polarised, so id-id forces are stronger (5.4.1).

book_ref.quote: in a larger atom or molecule the dispersion of electronic cloud and polarisation is relatively easier

blocks.prompt: 37 At room conditions, bromine is a:
blocks.explanation: F₂ and Cl₂ are gases, bromine is a liquid and iodine a solid, as size and polarizability increase (5.4.1).

book_ref.quote: The first two members in the halogen family (F₂ and Cl₂) are gases

blocks.prompt: 38 According to Table 5.1, the boiling points of the noble gases:
blocks.explanation: Boiling points rise from He (4.22 K) to Xe (165 K) with increasing molecular mass and size (5.4.1).

book_ref.quote: This factor operates in the halogen and noble gas families.

blocks.prompt: 39 Using Table 5.1, the difference between the boiling points of I₂ (458 K) and Cl₂ (239 K) is:
blocks.explanation: 458 − 239 = 219 K; the larger I₂ molecule has stronger London forces (5.4.1).

book_ref.quote: The physical state changes in the halogen family from top to bottom

blocks.prompt: 40 A molecule with a larger surface area has stronger intermolecular forces because it:

options.text: has more contacts with nearby molecules

blocks.explanation: Larger surface area gives more points of contact with neighbouring molecules, so forces are stronger (5.4.1).

book_ref.quote: A molecule with larger surface area has more number of contacts for a nearby molecule.

blocks.prompt: 41 The boiling point of hexane (C₆H₁₄) is 68.7 °C and that of ethane (C₂H₆) is −88.6 °C. The difference is:
blocks.explanation: 68.7 − (−88.6) = 157.3 °C; the longer chain of hexane has stronger attractive forces (5.4.1).

book_ref.quote: Compare the length of the chains in C₂H₆ and C₆H₁₄.

blocks.prompt: 42 Among the isomers of pentane, the highest boiling point is shown by:
blocks.explanation: Straight-chain n-pentane has the largest surface area and so the highest boiling point (5.4.1).

book_ref.quote: Straight chain pentane has largest surface area and so is its boiling point among the three isomers of pentane.

blocks.prompt: 43 The weakest intermolecular forces among the pentane isomers occur in:
blocks.explanation: Neopentane has the smallest surface area, so the least strong forces (5.4.1).

book_ref.quote: the least strong forces occur in 2,2-Dimethylpropane

blocks.prompt: 44 According to Table 5.2, which hydrocarbon is a liquid at S.T.P.?
blocks.explanation: Methane to butane are gases; pentane (b.p. 36.1 °C) is a liquid (5.4.1).

book_ref.quote: Boiling points of some hydrocarbons are given in Table 5.2.

blocks.prompt: 45 The three isomers of pentane differ in boiling point although they have the same Mᵣ because they differ in:
blocks.explanation: Same Mᵣ but different surface areas give different strengths of London forces (5.4.1).

book_ref.quote: Three isomers of pentane have the same relative molecular mass

blocks.prompt: 46 The attraction between the positive end of one polar molecule and the negative end of a nearby polar molecule is a:
blocks.explanation: This is the definition of the permanent dipole-permanent dipole force (5.4.2).

book_ref.quote: The force of attraction between the positive end of a polar molecule and the negative end of a nearby polar molecule

blocks.prompt: 47 Which pair of substances shows permanent dipole-permanent dipole forces as described in the chapter?
blocks.explanation: HCl molecules line up in the liquid; similar forces are present in chloroform (CHCl₃) (5.4.2).

book_ref.quote: Whenever the HCl molecules are close to each other (as in liquid state)

blocks.prompt: 48 In a chloroform molecule the negative centre lies:

options.text: on the end with the Cl atoms

blocks.explanation: Chloroform has a positive centre at H and a negative centre at the end with the Cl atoms (5.4.2).

book_ref.quote: The molecule of chloroform has a positive center at the H atom

blocks.prompt: 49 A hydrogen bond is a special type of:
blocks.explanation: Hydrogen bond is a special type of dipole-dipole force (5.4.3).

book_ref.quote: Hydrogen bond is a special type of dipole-dipole force.

blocks.prompt: 50 Which statement about the hydrogen bond is correct?

options.text: It is the strongest intermolecular force but weaker than ionic, metallic and covalent bonds
It is stronger than a covalent bond
It is the weakest intermolecular force
It is as strong as an ionic bond

blocks.explanation: The hydrogen bond is the strongest intermolecular force, yet weaker than all major bonds (5.4.3).

book_ref.quote: It is the strongest force among intermolecular forces

blocks.prompt: 51 The strength of a hydrogen bond is about:

options.text: one tenth of an ordinary covalent bond

blocks.explanation: A hydrogen bond, shown by a dotted line, has one tenth the strength of an ordinary covalent bond (5.4.3).

book_ref.quote: its strength is one tenth of an ordinary covalent bond

blocks.prompt: 52 A hydrogen bond can form when hydrogen is bonded to:

options.text: F, O or N carrying a lone pair

blocks.explanation: Hydrogen must be attached to a highly electronegative atom (F, O or N) that has a lone pair (5.4.3).

book_ref.quote: The hydrogen atom is connected to a highly electronegative atom, such as F, O, or N

blocks.prompt: 53 On average, one water molecule can form how many hydrogen bonds according to the chapter?
blocks.explanation: Water has two H atoms and two lone pairs on O, so it forms two hydrogen bonds on average (5.4.3).

book_ref.quote: A water molecule contains two hydrogen atoms and two lone pairs on oxygen.

blocks.prompt: 54 Ammonia forms only one hydrogen bond per molecule because:

options.text: NH₃ has only one H atom
N has only one lone pair

blocks.explanation: Despite three H atoms, NH₃ has only one lone pair on N, so only one H-bond per molecule (5.4.3).

book_ref.quote: ammonia can form only one hydrogen bond per molecule despite having three hydrogen atoms

blocks.prompt: 55 HF forms only one hydrogen bond per molecule because:

options.text: it has only one H atom
F has only one lone pair

blocks.explanation: F has three lone pairs, but HF has only one H atom, so it is restricted to one bond (5.4.3).

book_ref.quote: It has three lone pairs on the F atom which allows it to form three H-bonds.

blocks.prompt: 56 The boiling point of HF is higher than that of NH₃ because:

options.text: the hydrogen bond in HF is stronger owing to the high electronegativity of F

blocks.explanation: HF's hydrogen bond is stronger than NH₃'s owing to F's high electronegativity: b.p. 19.9 °C vs −33.5 °C (5.4.3).

book_ref.quote: Thus, its b.p (19.9℃) is much higher than ammonia (–33.5℃).

blocks.prompt: 57 In the solid state, HF molecules are joined by hydrogen bonds in a:
blocks.explanation: Solid HF molecules join in a zig-zag manner through hydrogen bonds (5.4.3).

book_ref.quote: The molecules of HF join with one other in a zig-zag manner in solid form

blocks.prompt: 58 The low acidic strength of HF compared with HCl, HBr and HI is due to:

options.text: strong hydrogen bonding that entraps the hydrogen

blocks.explanation: Partially positive H is entrapped between two highly electronegative F atoms by strong hydrogen bonding (5.4.3).

book_ref.quote: The exceptional low acidic strength of HF molecule as compared to HCl, HBr and HI

blocks.text: 5.4.4 Influence of hydrogen bonding on the properties of water

blocks.prompt: 59 Water has a high specific heat capacity because of its:
blocks.explanation: Water's unique structure allows strong hydrogen bonds, giving a high specific heat capacity (5.4.4).

book_ref.quote: Water has a high specific heat capacity.

blocks.prompt: 60 From H₂S to H₂Po the enthalpy change of vaporization:
blocks.explanation: Group 16 hydrides H₂S to H₂Po show a regular increase, because London forces grow with atomic size (5.4.4).

book_ref.quote: The general trend of enthalpy change of vaporization of group 16 hydrides is a regular increase from H₂S to H₂Po

blocks.prompt: 61 If water followed the trend of the other group 16 hydrides, its heat of vaporization would be:
blocks.explanation: Being the smallest hydride, water would have the lowest value; hydrogen bonding makes it the highest (5.4.4).

book_ref.quote: If water had followed this trend, the heat of vaporization of water would be the lowest

blocks.prompt: 62 The high surface tension of water is due to the pull on surface molecules by:
blocks.explanation: The downward pull is caused by attraction of the inner molecules through hydrogen bonds (5.4.4).

book_ref.quote: This downward pull is due to the attraction of inner molecules through hydrogen bonds.

blocks.prompt: 63 Water has a higher viscosity than hexane because:

options.text: hexane has a higher molar mass
hexane cannot form hydrogen bonds while water is strongly hydrogen bonded

blocks.explanation: Water's high viscosity is due to strong hydrogen bonds; hydrocarbons cannot form hydrogen bonds (5.4.4).

book_ref.quote: Hydrocarbons lack the ability to make the hydrogen bond.

blocks.prompt: 64 In the tetrahedral structure of a water molecule, the two lone pairs of oxygen occupy:
blocks.explanation: Two lone pairs on oxygen occupy two corners of the tetrahedron (5.4.4).

book_ref.quote: The molecules of water have tetrahedral structure.

blocks.prompt: 65 When water freezes it occupies about:
blocks.explanation: Empty spaces in the hydrogen-bonded ice structure make it occupy 9% more space, lowering density (5.4.4).

book_ref.quote: This is why, when water freezes, it occupies 9% more space and its density decreases.

blocks.prompt: 66 If 200 cm³ of water freezes and ice occupies 9% more space, the volume of ice formed is:

book_ref.quote: Empty spaces are created in the extensively hydrogen-bonded structure

blocks.prompt: 67 Fish survive under frozen lakes because:

options.text: less dense ice floats and insulates the water beneath

blocks.explanation: Ice floats as a blanket due to its low density and insulates the water beneath (5.4.4).

book_ref.quote: the fish and other living creatures survive under the frozen lakes and oceans

blocks.prompt: 68 Surface tension makes the surface of a liquid behave like:
blocks.explanation: Surface tension is the force along the surface that makes it behave like an elastic sheet (5.5).

book_ref.quote: causing it to behave like an elastic sheet

blocks.prompt: 69 Liquid droplets are spherical because:

options.text: surface tension makes liquids minimise their surface area

blocks.explanation: Surface tension makes liquids minimise surface area, so droplets form spheres (5.5).

book_ref.quote: Liquids tend to minimize their surface area due to surface tension, which explains why droplets form spheres.

blocks.prompt: 70 Molecules at the surface of a liquid experience a net force:
blocks.explanation: Surface molecules feel a net inward force due to intermolecular forces, forming a 'skin' (5.5).

book_ref.quote: Molecules at the surface experience a net force inward due to intermolecular forces

blocks.prompt: 71 Which of the following is influenced by surface tension according to the chapter?
blocks.explanation: Surface tension influences capillary action, wetting, and formation of droplets and bubbles (5.5).

book_ref.quote: Surface tension influences various phenomena, such as, capillary action

blocks.prompt: 72 When the temperature of a liquid is increased, its surface tension usually:
blocks.explanation: Surface tension typically decreases with increasing temperature (5.5).

book_ref.quote: Surface tension typically decreases with increasing temperature.

blocks.prompt: 73 According to Table 5.3, which liquid has the highest surface tension at 20 °C?
blocks.explanation: Water has γ = 72.75 × 10⁻³ N m⁻¹, far above the others, due to hydrogen bonding (5.5).

book_ref.quote: Table 5.3 Surface tension of some liquids at 20 °C in N m⁻¹

blocks.prompt: 74 The surface tension of benzene at 20 °C is 28.85 × 10⁻³ N m⁻¹. In dynes cm⁻¹ it is:
blocks.explanation: As 72.75 × 10⁻³ N m⁻¹ = 72.75 dynes cm⁻¹ for water, 28.85 × 10⁻³ N m⁻¹ = 28.85 dynes cm⁻¹ (5.5).

book_ref.quote: ‘γ’ are values multiple of 10⁻³ = 1/1000.

blocks.prompt: 75 Stronger intermolecular forces in a liquid lead to:
blocks.explanation: Stronger intermolecular forces give higher surface tension (5.5).

book_ref.quote: Intermolecular forces: Stronger intermolecular forces lead to higher surface tension.

blocks.prompt: 76 When stirred water is left undisturbed in a beaker, which layer comes to rest first?

options.text: the layer next to the walls
all layers at the same time

blocks.explanation: The layer adjacent to the walls stops first and the layer near the centre stops last (5.6).

book_ref.quote: the liquid layer adjacent to the walls of the beaker comes to rest first

blocks.prompt: 77 The resistance to the flow of a liquid is called:
blocks.explanation: Resistance to flow, a frictional force between adjacent layers, is viscosity (5.6).

book_ref.quote: This resistance to the flow of a liquid is termed as viscosity.

blocks.prompt: 78 The SI unit of viscosity is:
blocks.explanation: SI unit of viscosity is kg m⁻¹ s⁻¹; N m⁻¹ is the unit used for surface tension (5.6).

book_ref.quote: In international system (SI), unit of viscosity is in kg m⁻¹ s⁻¹.

blocks.prompt: 79 In the CGS system, viscosity is measured in:
blocks.explanation: The CGS unit of viscosity is the poise (P) (5.6).

book_ref.quote: In CGS system, the unit of viscosity is poise (P).

blocks.prompt: 80 Increasing the temperature of a liquid:

options.text: turns it into a liquid crystal

blocks.explanation: Higher temperature raises average KE, letting molecules overcome attractions, which lowers viscosity (5.6.1).

book_ref.quote: This lowers the viscosity.

blocks.prompt: 81 Liquids with stronger intermolecular forces have greater viscosity because their molecules:

options.text: cannot move around each other freely

blocks.explanation: Strong forces stop molecules moving around each other freely, so resistance to flow increases (5.6.1).

book_ref.quote: the greater the viscosity of liquids because liquid molecules cannot move around each other freely

blocks.prompt: 82 Evaporation is the spontaneous conversion of a liquid into vapour:
blocks.explanation: Evaporation occurs at any temperature, unlike boiling (5.7).

book_ref.quote: Evaporation is the spontaneous conversion of a liquid into vapour at any temperature.

blocks.prompt: 83 Evaporation causes cooling because:

options.text: the liquid absorbs heat from its vapour
high-energy molecules leave and low-energy molecules are left behind

blocks.explanation: Loss of high-energy molecules lowers the temperature of the liquid; heat then flows from the surroundings (5.7).

book_ref.quote: When high energy molecules leave the liquid and low energy molecules are left behind

blocks.prompt: 84 Earthenware vessels keep water cool because they are:

options.text: porous, so water evaporates through the pores

blocks.explanation: Earthenware is porous; water escapes through pores and evaporates, lowering the average KE of the remaining water (5.7).

book_ref.quote: Earthenware vessels keep water cooler under the same phenomenon.

blocks.prompt: 85 The recapture of vapour molecules by the surface of the liquid is called:
blocks.explanation: Vapour molecules recaptured by the liquid surface undergo condensation (5.8).

book_ref.quote: There are chances that these molecules are recaptured by the surface of liquid.

blocks.prompt: 86 In a closed vessel, equilibrium is reached when:

options.text: rate of evaporation equals rate of condensation

blocks.explanation: Both processes continue until their rates become equal (5.8).

book_ref.quote: the rate of evaporation becomes equal to the rate of condensation

blocks.prompt: 87 Vapour pressure is the pressure exerted by the vapour:

options.text: in equilibrium with its liquid at a given temperature
of a liquid at its boiling point only

blocks.explanation: Vapour pressure is exerted by vapour in equilibrium with its liquid at a given temperature (5.8).

book_ref.quote: The pressure exerted by the liquid vapour in equilibrium with its liquid at a given temperature is called vapour pressure.

blocks.prompt: 88 The vapour pressure of a liquid at a given temperature depends on:

options.text: the nature of the liquid (its intermolecular forces)
the surface area of the liquid

blocks.explanation: Vapour pressure does not depend on amount, container volume or surface area; it depends on intermolecular forces (5.8, 5.9.1).

book_ref.quote: The magnitude of vapour pressure does not depend upon the amount of liquid in the container

blocks.prompt: 89 A larger surface area does not change the vapour pressure because:

options.text: the rate of condensation also increases

blocks.explanation: A larger surface area is also a larger target for returning molecules, so condensation increases too (5.8).

book_ref.quote: The larger surface area presents a larger target for returning the molecules

blocks.prompt: 90 As a liquid is heated, its vapour pressure:

options.text: first rises then falls to zero

blocks.explanation: On heating, vapour pressure keeps increasing (Figure 5.9: water, ethyl alcohol, ethylene glycol, diethyl ether) (5.9).

book_ref.quote: The Figure 5.9 shows the variation of vapour pressure of water, ethyl alcohol, ethylene glycol and diethyl ether

blocks.prompt: 91 At the boiling point, further heating:

options.text: breaks intermolecular forces without raising the temperature
turns the liquid into a solid

blocks.explanation: Extra heat at the boiling point breaks intermolecular forces and converts liquid to vapour; temperature stays constant (5.9).

book_ref.quote: Any further heating at this stage will not increase the temperature.

blocks.prompt: 92 At the boiling point bubbles come out of the liquid because their internal pressure is:

options.text: greater than the atmospheric pressure on the surface
equal to the pressure of the container walls

blocks.explanation: Vapour bubbles in the interior have greater internal pressure than the atmospheric pressure on the surface (5.9).

book_ref.quote: the bubbles of vapour which are formed in the interior of the liquid have greater internal pressure

blocks.prompt: 93 At sea level, liquids reach their boiling points when their vapour pressure equals:
blocks.explanation: Figure 5.9 shows liquids boil when vapour pressure reaches 760 torr at sea level (5.9).

book_ref.quote: the liquids reach upto their boiling points when their vapour pressures are equal to 760 torr at sea level

blocks.prompt: 94 Stronger intermolecular forces in a liquid give:

options.text: higher vapour pressure and lower boiling point
higher vapour pressure and higher boiling point
lower vapour pressure and higher boiling point

blocks.explanation: Stronger forces mean lower vapour pressure and higher boiling point (5.9.1).

book_ref.quote: Stronger the intermolecular forces, lower will be the vapour pressure and higher will be the boiling point.

blocks.prompt: 95 According to Table 5.4, which liquid has the lowest boiling point at 1 atm?
blocks.explanation: CS₂ boils at 46.30 °C, the lowest in Table 5.4 (5.9.1).

book_ref.quote: Table 5.4 Boiling points of some common liquids at 760 torr (1 atm.)

blocks.prompt: 96 Water (b.p. 100 °C) boils at a higher temperature than ethanol (b.p. 78.3 °C). This shows that water has:
blocks.explanation: A higher boiling point indicates stronger intermolecular forces in water than in ethanol (5.9.1).

book_ref.quote: Higher boiling point of H₂O indicates stronger intermolecular forces than that of ethanol

blocks.prompt: 97 When the external pressure on a liquid is increased, its boiling point:
blocks.explanation: At higher external pressure more heat is needed to make vapour pressure equal to it, so boiling point is raised (5.9.1).

book_ref.quote: When the external pressure is high the liquid requires greater amount of heat

blocks.prompt: 98 Water boils at 25 °C when the external pressure is:
blocks.explanation: Water boils at 25 °C at 23.7 torr and at 120 °C at 1489 torr (5.9.1).

book_ref.quote: water shows B.P of 120 °C at 1489 torr pressure and boils at 25 °C at 23.7 torr

blocks.prompt: 99 Water boils at 98 °C at Murree hills because:

options.text: the external pressure there is 1489 torr
the external pressure there is only 700 torr
water there has no hydrogen bonds

blocks.explanation: At Murree the external pressure is 700 torr, lower than 760 torr, so water boils below 100 °C (5.9.1).

book_ref.quote: Water boils at 98 °C at Murree hills due to external pressure of 700 torr

blocks.prompt: 100 Food cooks quickly in a pressure cooker because:

options.text: the boiling point of water is lowered
water evaporates faster at low pressure
increased pressure raises the boiling point of water

blocks.explanation: Vapour is not allowed to escape, pressure rises, the boiling temperature increases and more heat is absorbed (5.9.1).

book_ref.quote: Pressure cooker is a closed container.

blocks.prompt: 101 The energy change accompanying a physical change is a quantitative measure of the difference in:
blocks.explanation: The energy change measures the difference in the strength of intermolecular forces (5.10).

book_ref.quote: This change in energy is the quantitative measurement of the difference in the strength of intermolecular forces.

blocks.prompt: 102 The heat absorbed by one mole of a solid to melt it at its melting point at 1 atm is called:
blocks.explanation: This is the definition of molar heat of fusion, ΔHf (5.10).

book_ref.quote: The amount of heat absorbed by one mole of a solid to melt it into the liquid at its melting point

blocks.prompt: 103 The molar heat of fusion of ice at 0 °C (accepted value) is:
blocks.explanation: The accepted ΔHf of ice is 6.01 kJ mol⁻¹ (the printed 4.6 is corrected in the chapter) (5.10).

book_ref.quote: The accepted value is 6.01 kJ mol⁻¹ at 0 °C

blocks.prompt: 104 Heat needed to melt 3.0 mol of ice at 0 °C is: (ΔHf = 6.01 kJ mol⁻¹)

book_ref.quote: H₂O(s) → H₂O(l), ΔHf = 6.01 kJ mol⁻¹.

blocks.prompt: 105 Molar heat of vaporization is measured at:
blocks.explanation: It is the heat absorbed by one mole of liquid to become vapour at its boiling point at 1 atm (5.10).

book_ref.quote: to convert it into one mole of vapour at its boiling point at 1 atmospheric pressure

blocks.prompt: 106 Molar heat of vaporization of a liquid depends upon:
blocks.explanation: Molar heat of vaporization depends on the strength of intermolecular forces (5.10).

book_ref.quote: The molar heats of vaportization depends upon the strength of intermolecular forces.

blocks.prompt: 107 How much heat is absorbed when 2.5 mol of water is vaporized at 100 °C? (ΔHv = 40.6 kJ mol⁻¹)

book_ref.quote: When one mole H₂O is converted to vapour at 100 °C, then heat absorbed is 40.6 kJ mol⁻¹.

blocks.prompt: 108 Using the chapter's values (H₂O 40.6, NH₃ 21.7 kJ mol⁻¹), the molar heat of vaporization of water is about how many times that of NH₃?
blocks.explanation: 40.6/21.7 = 1.87 ≈ 1.9; water's intermolecular forces are much stronger (5.10).

book_ref.quote: NH₃ and HCl only need 21.7 and 15.6 kJ mol⁻¹ respectively

blocks.prompt: 109 Heat needed to vaporize 2.0 mol of NH₃ at its boiling point is: (ΔHv = 21.7 kJ mol⁻¹)

book_ref.quote: This difference is due to the stronger intermolecular forces in water.

blocks.prompt: 110 When a solid absorbs its molar heat of fusion, its particles:

options.text: move away from one another and gain freedom to move

blocks.explanation: Absorbed energy lets particles move apart, changing the state and giving freedom to move and rotate (5.10).

book_ref.quote: Particles gain more freedom to move and rotate in the liquid and gas phase.

blocks.prompt: 111 Solids are substances that have:

options.text: no definite shape but definite volume
definite shape but no definite volume

blocks.explanation: Solids are rigid, hard and have definite shape and volume (5.11).

book_ref.quote: Solids are those substances which are rigid, hard, have definite shape and definite volume.

blocks.prompt: 112 In hexagonal and cubic close-packed metallic solids, spherical particles cannot occupy more than:
blocks.explanation: Spherical particles in close packing occupy at most 74% of space, so compression of solids is not possible (5.11).

book_ref.quote: they cannot occupy more than 74% space

blocks.prompt: 113 Solids cannot be compressed because their particles:

options.text: are already closely packed and touch each other

blocks.explanation: Solid particles are closely packed with outer boundaries touching; they cannot move closer (5.11).

book_ref.quote: It means the compression of solids is not possible.

blocks.prompt: 114 Increase in temperature hardly increases the volume of a solid because:

options.text: the forces of attraction are very strong

blocks.explanation: In solids the forces are so strong that heating hardly affects relative positions of particles (5.11).

book_ref.quote: Increase in temperature of solids hardly increases their volume.

blocks.prompt: 115 The constituent particles of a solid:

options.text: only vibrate about their mean positions

blocks.explanation: Solid particles have no translatory or rotational motion; they only vibrate about mean positions (5.11).

book_ref.quote: They only vibrate about their mean positions.

blocks.prompt: 116 At higher temperature, the vibrations of particles in a solid:
blocks.explanation: Vibrations about mean positions become more intense at higher temperature (5.11).

book_ref.quote: These vibrations become more intense at higher temperature.

blocks.prompt: 117 Because their particles are closely packed, solids are mostly:

options.text: hard with high melting points and high stability

blocks.explanation: Close packing makes solids mostly hard, with high melting points and high stability (5.11).

book_ref.quote: Due to closely packed atoms, molecules, and ions, solids are mostly hard

blocks.prompt: 118 In solids, the particles are held together by:

options.text: ionic, covalent, metallic or van der Waals forces

blocks.explanation: Solid particles are held by ionic, covalent, metallic or van der Waals forces (5.11).

book_ref.quote: held together by ionic, covalent, metallic or van der Waals forces

blocks.prompt: 119 The only kinetic energy possessed by solids is:
blocks.explanation: Solid particles only vibrate, so their only KE is vibrational (5.11).

book_ref.quote: the only kinetic energy that solids possess is vibrational kinetic energy

blocks.prompt: 120 On the basis of arrangement of particles, solids are of:
blocks.explanation: Solids are crystalline or amorphous on the basis of particle arrangement (5.12).

book_ref.quote: There are two types of solids on the basis of the way their particles are arranged

blocks.prompt: 121 The regular arrangement of ions, atoms or molecules in three-dimensional space is called:
blocks.explanation: This defines the crystal lattice (5.12.1).

book_ref.quote: The regular arrangement of ions, atoms, or molecules in three dimensional space

blocks.prompt: 122 Which of the following is a crystalline solid?
blocks.explanation: Diamond, sodium chloride and ice are crystalline; glass, plastic sulphur and charcoal are amorphous (5.12.1, 5.12.2).

book_ref.quote: For example, diamond, sodium chloride, ice, etc.

blocks.prompt: 123 For a given crystal, the interfacial angles at which surfaces intersect:

options.text: change with the size of the crystal
are always the same whatever shape it is grown in

blocks.explanation: Interfacial angles are always the same and remain characteristic even in fine powder (5.12.1).

book_ref.quote: the interfacial angles, at which the surfaces intersect, are always the same

blocks.prompt: 124 Crystalline solids can be identified from their:

options.text: ability to be blown into shapes

blocks.explanation: Crystalline solids have sharp melting points and can be identified by them (5.12.1).

book_ref.quote: Crystalline solids have sharp melting points.

blocks.prompt: 125 The definite planes along which crystalline solids break are called:
blocks.explanation: Crystalline solids break along definite cleavage planes inclined at a particular angle (5.12.1).

book_ref.quote: These planes are called the cleavage planes

blocks.prompt: 126 Crystals can be grown from a saturated solution by:

options.text: slow evaporation of the solvent or seeding

blocks.explanation: Crystal growth is done by slow evaporation of the solvent or by seeding (5.12.1).

book_ref.quote: This can be done by slow evaporation of the solvent or by seeding process from saturated solution.

blocks.prompt: 127 When a small crystal of Na₂S₂O₃ is added to its supersaturated solution:
blocks.explanation: A supersaturated solution is not in equilibrium with the solid; adding a seed crystal causes rapid crystallization (5.12.1).

book_ref.quote: if small crystal of Na₂S₂O₃ is added to super saturated solution, the crystallization happens rapidly

blocks.prompt: 128 The shape in which a crystal usually grows is called its:
blocks.explanation: The usual growth shape of a crystal is its habit; it may change if growing conditions change (5.12.1).

book_ref.quote: The shape of a crystal in which it usually grows is called habit of a crystal.

blocks.prompt: 129 Small regions of orderly arrangement of particles in an amorphous solid are called:
blocks.explanation: Amorphous solids may have small ordered regions, crystallites, but no long-range regularity (5.12.2).

book_ref.quote: The regions where orderly arrangement of particles is present are known as crystallites.

blocks.prompt: 130 Glass melts:
blocks.explanation: Amorphous solids like glass melt over a wide range of temperature (5.12.2).

book_ref.quote: Amorphous solids like glass melts over a wide temperature range.

blocks.prompt: 131 Amorphous solids do not have a definite value of:
blocks.explanation: Amorphous solids do not have a definite value of heat of fusion (5.12.2).

book_ref.quote: Amorphous solids do not have definite value of heat of fusion.

blocks.prompt: 132 Crystalline solids are anisotropic. This means their properties:

options.text: depend upon the direction of measurement
are the same in all directions
change with the amount of solid

blocks.explanation: Anisotropic: properties depend on the direction of measurement; amorphous solids are isotropic (Table 5.5) (5.12.2).

book_ref.quote: It means that their properties depend upon the direction along which the measurements are made.

blocks.prompt: 133 Amorphous solids such as glass can be:

options.text: moulded and blown into different shapes
grown by seeding into identical crystals
melted only at a sharp temperature

blocks.explanation: Amorphous solids can be moulded and blown to form different shapes (5.12.2).

book_ref.quote: They can be molded and blown to form different shapes.

blocks.prompt: 134 Which of the following is NOT an amorphous solid?
blocks.explanation: Glass, wood, plastic sulphur, charcoal, coal and coke are amorphous; NaCl is crystalline (5.12.2).

book_ref.quote: The examples of amorphous solids are glass, wood, amorphous sulphur (plastic sulphur)

blocks.prompt: 135 Liquid crystals are substances that:

options.text: are neither fully liquid nor fully solid

blocks.explanation: At certain temperatures many substances exist in a phase neither fully liquid nor fully solid (5.13).

book_ref.quote: many substances exist in a phase that is neither fully liquid nor fully solid

blocks.prompt: 136 In most liquid crystals the rod-like molecules have a length about:

options.text: four to eight times their diameter

blocks.explanation: Most liquid crystal molecules are rigid rods 4-8 times longer than their diameter (5.13).

book_ref.quote: a length four to eight times greater than their diameter

blocks.prompt: 137 Molecules of a liquid crystal can:

options.text: spin around their long axis but not rotate end over end

blocks.explanation: Molecules can migrate and spin about the long axis but cannot rotate end over end (5.13).

book_ref.quote: They can spin around their long axis, but they can’t rotate end over end.

blocks.prompt: 138 When packed together, liquid crystal molecules orient with their long axes roughly parallel, like:

options.text: logs in a stack of firewood

blocks.explanation: They line up roughly parallel like logs in a stack of firewood (5.13).

book_ref.quote: like logs in a stack of firewood

blocks.prompt: 139 Liquid crystals show optical properties like those of:
blocks.explanation: Liquid crystals flow and show viscosity like liquids, but show optical properties like crystals and are always anisotropic (5.13.1).

book_ref.quote: show optical properties like crystals.

blocks.prompt: 140 Which property of liquid crystals resembles solids?

options.text: They are somewhat rigid with a parallel ordered arrangement

blocks.explanation: Parallel ordered arrangement and some rigidity resemble crystals; flowing and viscosity resemble liquids (5.13.1).

book_ref.quote: have parallel ordered arrangement.

blocks.prompt: 141 The main application area of liquid crystals is:
blocks.explanation: Electro-optic devices are electrically controlled devices that modulate light (5.13.2).

book_ref.quote: The main application area of liquid crystals is in electro-optic devices.

blocks.prompt: 142 Cholesteric liquid crystals help locate a tumour because the tumour is:
blocks.explanation: A tumour has a different (higher) temperature than surrounding tissue, which liquid crystals detect (5.13.2).

book_ref.quote: When cholesteric liquid crystals are applied to the breast, a tumor is located because of being warmer

blocks.prompt: 143 Liquid crystal temperature sensors can find faulty connections on a circuit board by detecting:

options.text: a change of colour of copper

blocks.explanation: Faulty connections show a characteristic higher temperature detected by liquid crystal sensors (5.13.2).

book_ref.quote: Liquid crystal temperature sensors can also be used to find faulty connections on a circuit board

blocks.prompt: 144 The most common application of liquid crystal technology is:
blocks.explanation: LCDs in TV, laptops, cell phones, calculators and watches are the most common application (5.13.2).

book_ref.quote: The most common application of liquid crystal technology is liquid crystal displays
